query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Zr content in a refractory high-entropy alloy processed by direct energy deposition (DED) will enhance elevated-temperature yield strength by promoting solid solution strengthening and stabilizing grain boundaries against coarsening.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally deposited refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbTiAlZrHfTaMoW with standard Zr concentration) produced by DED with a baseline fine-grained B2 matrix.
generation.intervention: Increase the Zr concentration beyond the conventional formulation during powder blending prior to DED deposition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing at temperatures in the range of 1023 K to 1123 K under load-bearing conditions typical of extreme environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and grain boundary segregation caused by the additional Zr, which reinforces the B2 matrix and impedes dislocation movement.
generation.mechanism: The extra Zr increases solid solution strengthening by introducing greater atomic size mismatch and localized lattice strain, thereby inhibiting dislocation motion at elevated temperatures and delaying grain growth or coarsening.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable increase in yield strength and hardness at 1023 K and 1123 K compared to the baseline alloy with standard Zr content.
generation.baseline: The mechanically characterized as-deposited refractory HEA with conventional Zr content (e.g., as reported in baseline compositions using DED).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under high-temperature conditions (around 1023–1123 K) for load-bearing structural applications; the effect may not hold at temperatures significantly above 1223 K or in radically different processing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement and the optimal Zr concentration are uncertain without further systematic compositional studies, and there is potential trade-off with ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples using DED: one set with the baseline Zr concentration and one set with elevated Zr content. Ensure all other processing parameters and compositions are identical. Perform high-temperature tensile and hardness tests at 1023 K and 1123 K to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Hardness via microindentation at elevated temperatures
Grain size and phase distribution via SEM/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with increased Zr content do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or hardness (i.e., no measurable difference beyond experimental uncertainty) compared to the baseline samples at 1023 K and 1123 K, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTiAlZrHfTaMoW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) system with the structure of the B2 matrix (antiphase domains) and antiphase domain boundaries was firstly developed. We conducted the mechanical properties of the RHEAs at 298 K, 1023 K, 1123 K, and 1223 K, as well as typical deformation characteristics. The RHEAs with low density (7.41~7.51 g/cm3) have excellent compressive-specific yield strength (σYS/ρ) at 1023 K (~131 MPa·cm3/g) and 1123 K (~104.2 MPa·cm3/g), respectively, which are far superior to most typical RHEAs. And, they still keep appropriate plastic deformability at room temperature (ε > 0.35). The superior specific yield strengths are mainly attributed to the solid solution strengthening induced by the Zr element. The formation of the dislocation slip bands with [111](101_) and [111](112_) directions and their interaction provide considerable plastic deformation capability. Meanwhile, dynamic recrystallization and dislocation annihilation accelerate the continuous softening after yielding at 1123 K.Keywords: refractory high-entropy alloys, B2 phase, specific yield strength, strain softening, deformation microstructure

In this study, a Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEA was deposited using DED. The phase diagram and phase fraction of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were analyzed for deposition on Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. For the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, powders of each element were mixed to prepare a mixed Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al powder and deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates. The microstructure and hardness of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were measured. In addition, HAZ and thermal shielding analyses were performed on the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. The primary findings of this study are as follows: SEM images and EBSD analysis were used to investigate the microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. Phase analysis predicted that the BCC B2 phase was 62.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 21.6%, and C14 Laves phase was 16.2%. However, the σ phase was 64.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 28.2%, and the Ti2Ni phase was 7.6% in the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.The microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al consisted of a phase not predicted by the phase analysis but showed a microstructure similar to that of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al annealed after casting. In addition, the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al exhibited a fine grain size of 1–35 μm.
